passage: The washing machines at the laundrette in Leeds hummed while Ada, nine, flipped through a crumpled kids' magazine someone had left on the bench. She found her star sign and read it under her breath: "You are kind, but sometimes shy. You have a secret talent people haven't noticed yet." Ada gasped and tugged her brother's sleeve. "Yosef, listen! That's exactly me. I'm kind to the cat, and I was shy at the party on Saturday." Yosef, thirteen, was reading the next sign down. "Mine says I'm kind but sometimes quiet," he mumbled. Ada wasn't listening. She tore the page out carefully, folded it into her coat pocket and patted it twice.

qa.q: Where were Ada and Yosef when Ada read the horoscope?
qa.a: They were at the laundrette in Leeds, on the bench while the washing machines hummed.

qa.q: What does Ada folding the page into her pocket suggest she feels about the horoscope?
qa.a: She feels it truly describes her and wants to keep it, like proof that someone understood her. She has already matched "kind" to the cat and "shy" to the party. 😊

qa.q: At which moment could Ada have noticed that the words fit almost anyone, and how?
qa.a: When Yosef said his sign also called him kind but sometimes quiet. If she had stopped to compare the two, she might have seen the same lines fit both of them, and most people.

qa.q: How might Yosef see the horoscope differently after reading his own sign?
qa.a: Yosef has just read almost the same words under a different sign, so to him the lines may sound written for everyone rather than a message meant only for his sister.

grounding: A child reads a general horoscope line about being kind and shy and is sure it describes her exactly, missing that it fits others too.

passage: Library period, and Afreen had the new children's magazine before anyone else. She skipped the puzzles and went straight to the last page. "Pisces: You like to help others, but sometimes you keep your feelings inside." Her mouth fell open. That morning she had helped the librarian stack the returned books, and she had not told anyone that her tooth was wobbling. "Jagdish," she whispered across the table, "how do they know?" Jagdish leaned over. "Know what?" "About me! It's like they watched me all week." She copied the line into the back of her rough notebook in her neatest writing and drew a small star beside it. When the bell rang, she read it once more before closing the magazine.

qa.q: Which line did Afreen read under Pisces?
qa.a: "You like to help others, but sometimes you keep your feelings inside."

qa.q: Why does Afreen feel the magazine seems to know her?
qa.a: Afreen feels amazed and excited, because the line matches her own week, helping the librarian and keeping quiet about her wobbly tooth, so it seems written just for her.

qa.q: What question could Afreen ask herself before copying the line as a true description of her?
qa.a: She could ask whether Jagdish or anyone else at the table also helps people and sometimes keeps feelings inside. If the line fits them too, it is not really about her.

qa.q: What is it like for Jagdish to hear "how do they know?" without seeing the page?
qa.a: Jagdish is puzzled and has to ask "Know what?" To Jagdish it is just a magazine page until Afreen's excitement makes it seem special.

grounding: A child in a school library is convinced a vague horoscope line about helping others and hiding feelings describes her exactly.

passage: I'm Binita, and my little brother Divyansh is eight. On Sunday he found the horoscope box in the newspaper's children's corner and read his aloud at breakfast: "You are brave, though sometimes you feel shy with new people." He put his spoon down. "That's me! I'm brave on the big slide, and I was shy with the new tuition teacher." Then he ran to show Papa, holding the page with both hands. While he was gone, I read the other eleven boxes. Most of them said almost the same thing in different words. When he came back, he stuck the cutting on his cupboard door with tape. I'm not sure what he was thinking, but he kept glancing at it all afternoon.

qa.q: Where did Divyansh stick the cutting?
qa.a: He stuck it on his cupboard door with tape.

qa.q: What does Divyansh running to show Papa suggest he feels?
qa.a: He seems thrilled and sure the horoscope is about him, because he links "brave" to the big slide and "shy" to the new tuition teacher.

qa.q: What could Binita do next to help Divyansh notice the pattern without making fun of him?
qa.a: Binita could read a few of the other boxes aloud and ask which one sounds like him. Hearing nearly the same words under other signs might help him see they fit many people.

qa.q: How does Binita see the horoscope differently from Divyansh?
qa.a: Binita has read all twelve boxes and found them nearly the same, so to Binita it is general. To Divyansh it feels like a message written only for him.

grounding: A young boy is certain a newspaper horoscope about being brave but shy describes him exactly, while his sibling sees it fits almost anyone.

passage:
Saturday: at the barber shop in Madurai, Madhav, ten, waited his turn with an old children's magazine. On the back page was his sign: 'You are kind, but sometimes shy. You notice things others miss.' He read it three times. How did they know? He tore the corner off carefully and put it in his pocket.
Monday: at recess he showed it to Shankar. 'This is exactly me. I noticed the new boy had no pencil, remember?' Shankar shrugged. 'Okay.' Madhav smoothed the paper flat on his knee like a certificate.
Wednesday: the class teacher asked for volunteers for the school play. Madhav kept his hand down. At home he told his mother, 'It's not my fault. The magazine says I'm sometimes shy.'

qa.q: Where did Madhav find the horoscope?
qa.a: He found it on the back page of an old children's magazine at the barber shop in Madurai.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when he first read his sign?
qa.a: He felt amazed and understood, wondering how they knew, which is why he tore the corner off to keep it.

qa.q: What could Madhav do the next time he reads a line like that?
qa.a: He could read the other signs too and see if the same words fit Shankar or his mother, before letting it decide whether to join the school play.

qa.q: How might Madhav's mother feel when he blames the magazine for not volunteering?
qa.a: She might be surprised and a little worried that a general magazine line is now stopping him from trying something new.

grounding: A ten-year-old boy is sure a general magazine horoscope describes him exactly and even uses it to explain not volunteering.

passage: Sunaina, you're reading me your horoscope as if it were a letter written only to you. Come, sit with your Nandini Nani. When I was nine, in Shimla, my aunt kept film magazines under her bed. I wasn't supposed to read them, but I found the stars page. Mine said, 'You have a gentle heart, though you are sometimes shy with strangers.' I nearly cried. That was me! I was shy with the milkman! I copied it onto a slip and kept it in my geometry box for two whole years. Every exam, I'd open the box and read it for luck. I never once read the other signs. I didn't think to. Why would I? It was mine. Now, beti, read me what the other eleven say, and let's see how many of them are gentle and shy.

qa.q: Where did Nandini Nani keep the horoscope she copied?
qa.a: She kept it on a slip in her geometry box for two whole years.

qa.q: Why did young Nandini nearly cry when she read the stars page?
qa.a: She felt deeply seen, sure the line about a gentle heart and shyness was written about her alone, even the shyness with the milkman.

qa.q: What does Nani suggest Sunaina do, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Nani asks Sunaina to read the other eleven signs aloud, which will show whether the same kind of words would fit almost anyone.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel after hearing Nani's story?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel a bit caught out but also amused, seeing that Nani once treasured a line just like hers.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being certain at nine that a magazine horoscope described her exactly, never checking whether it fit anyone else.
